scenes.heading: Substituting integers into expressions
scenes.sub: What happens when x is negative?
scenes.say: If x equals negative three, is x squared nine or negative nine? In this video you'll learn how to put negative numbers into expressions and formulas without losing a sign.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A vending machine does the same steps, whatever coin goes in
scenes.science: An expression follows the same steps, whatever number you substitute
scenes.breaks: a machine only takes certain coins; an expression takes any number (just never divide by zero).
scenes.say: Think of an expression as a vending machine with a coin slot. Whatever you put in, the machine does the same steps in the same order. A negative number is just a different coin. Brackets are like the edges of the slot: they keep the whole coin, sign and all, together.

scenes.heading: The method
points: Swap each letter for its number in brackets
scenes.say: Here's the method. Swap each letter for its number, in brackets. Then follow BIDMAS. Remember that negative x means the opposite of x, so if x is negative, negative x is positive. And an even power is never negative.

scenes.heading: When x = −3
scenes.say: When x is negative three: x squared is nine, and two x squared is two times nine, eighteen. But negative x squared means square first, then apply the minus: negative nine. And two x, all squared, is negative six squared, thirty-six.
scenes.caption: When x = −3: x² = 9 and 2x² = 2 × 9 = 18. But −x² means square first, then apply the minus: −9. And (2x)² = (−6)² = 36.

scenes.heading: Power before minus
scenes.say: Watch negative x squared go through the machine, with x equal to negative three. First the square box: negative three squared is nine. Then the opposite box: the opposite of nine is negative nine. Squaring always comes before the minus out the front.
scenes.caption: −x² when x = −3: square first, (−3)² = 9, then take the opposite: −9.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Evaluate 2x² − 3x + 1 when x = −4.
scenes.say: Evaluate two x squared minus three x plus one when x is negative four. Substitute in brackets. Negative four squared is sixteen, and two times sixteen is thirty-two. Three times negative four is negative twelve, and subtracting negative twelve means add twelve. Thirty-two plus twelve plus one is forty-five.
scenes.caption: 2(−4)² − 3(−4) + 1. (−4)² = 16, so 2 × 16 = 32. 3 × (−4) = −12, and − (−12) = + 12. 32 + 12 + 1 = 45.

scenes.heading: A formula
scenes.question: T = 18 − 6h gives air temperature (°C) at height h km. Find T when h = 5.
scenes.say: A model for air temperature is T equals eighteen minus six h, where h is the height in kilometres. Five kilometres up: eighteen minus six times five is eighteen minus thirty, which is negative twelve degrees. Below freezing, which makes sense high in the sky.
scenes.caption: T = 18 − 6h. When h = 5: T = 18 − 6 × 5 = 18 − 30 = −12 °C. Below freezing, which makes sense high in the sky.

points: Bracket the swap, sign and all
x² is 9 but −x² is −9 when x = −3
−x is positive when x is negative
scenes.say: Quick recap. Bracket every number you substitute, then use BIDMAS. Watch the difference between x squared and negative x squared. And negative x is positive when x is negative. Now try the practice questions!
